📌 Session Keys: How Wallets Allow Actions Without Signing Every Time

Main Points
⏺ Session keys let apps perform limited actions without constant confirmations
⏺ They improve UX for games, trading, bots, and automation
⏺ This post explains why “no signature every time” needs strict limits

1️⃣ Core Idea — you pre-authorize an app to perform specific actions under defined rules.
2️⃣ Where It Helps — on-chain games, frequent trades, bots, subscriptions, and automated strategies.
3️⃣ Why It Matters — fewer popups, fewer manual approvals, smoother user experience.
4️⃣ Risk Surface — if permissions are too broad, the app gets dangerous control.
5️⃣ Practical Rule — limit amount, time, action type, and always read what you authorize.

Final Thoughts

Session keys make Web3 easier, but one approval can unlock many future actions. The wider the limit, the bigger the risk.

What does “gas” mean in crypto? 

“Gas” is important in the world of crypto. Simply put, gas is the payment needed when making a transaction or interacting with a smart contract on a blockchain — i.e., the network fee you pay. 

Gas is usually paid in the given blockchain’s native cryptocurrency — e.g., ETH is used for transactions on Ethereum, and BNB is used for the same on BNB Smart Chain). These fees go to miners or validators responsible for keeping networks secure and confirming transactions. Gas fees also prevent spam on the network, keeping the blockchain running smoothly.

Iran: Demands First, Hormuz Second 🛳


Iran said that any deal with Oman on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz would not lead to the waterway being fully reopened and that the route would remain closed until the United States agreed to demands including lifting a naval blockade.

The comments were the latest sign that Iran sees its grip on the strait — which has driven up global energy prices, creating a political headache for Trump — as its best form of leverage in negotiations with Washington.

Esmail Baghaei, spokesman for the Iranian Foreign Ministry, said at a news conference on Monday that the focus of the talks with Oman was “on reaching an understanding over a route for the safe passage of shipping,” Iranian state media reported.

The Oman talks were proceeding smoothly, Baghaei added, according to the reports, but “this issue is separate from the discussion of reopening the Strait of Hormuz,” which was “contingent upon the removal of the conditions that have been imposed on the Islamic Republic of Iran” by the United States.

The US and Iran are not negotiating directly, although Secretary of State Marco Rubio said last week that the talks between Iran and Oman were being conducted with American input.

The Strait of Hormuz, which runs between Iran and Oman, is a key route for the oil and gas trade. Tehran effectively closed the waterway after the United States and Israel launched their military campaign against Iran in late February, and it has become a key sticking point as Iran and the United States alternate between periods of negotiation and bursts of fighting.

The closure of the waterway has increased energy costs in the United States, where polls show that support for the already unpopular conflict is falling. 

Hard-liners in Iran believe that the country’s ability to close it to traffic has put it in a position of strength and that it should not make diplomatic concessions.

Last week, a top Iranian national security official issued a set of demands that are part of Iran’s longstanding public negotiating stance and that he said the United States must meet before Tehran would fully reopen the waterway.

Those included the lifting of the US naval blockade and sanctions on Iran, the withdrawal of American forces from around the country, the payment of war reparations, the release of frozen Iranian assets, and the end of attacks on Iran’s allies in the region.

Most of those demands were detailed in a cease-fire agreement, known as the Islamabad Memorandum, that the United States and Iran signed in June, though that document said sanctions would be fully lifted only in the event of a final deal regarding Iran’s nuclear program.

The June agreement quickly fell apart, and most of its terms were violated within weeks.

Trump has declared the deal “over.” On Sunday, he said that economic distress and high inflation in Iran would eventually force Tehran to agree to a new deal. He did not threaten further military action against Iran, saying, “We are low-keying it.”

📣 EU to revise MiCA rules in 2027 amid US stablecoin push 

⚠️ European Union officials are preparing to revise the bloc’s MiCA crypto framework in 2027 as foreign stablecoin restrictions and faster U.S. rulemaking expose gaps in the existing regime. The planned revision would examine how MiCA treats stablecoins issued outside the European Union. Current requirements have prevented several foreign issuers from receiving authorization, limiting their access to regulated exchanges across the bloc.

💬 “Reopening the file seems unavoidable at this stage,” an unidentified European diplomat told Euronews.

🔗 The diplomat cited positions taken by European institutions, including the European Central Bank, along with changes in global regulation and digital-asset technology. No final proposal has been published. Any amendment would need to pass through the EU’s legislative process before taking effect. The consultation covers developments that have occurred since MiCA entered into application. Its deadline has been extended to Sept. 30, with crypto issuers, service providers, regulators, central banks and finance ministries invited to respond.
